opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest way to describe it is that the architecture itself didn't change dramatically. DeepSeek V3 is still a decoder-style transformer. They made smart efficiency choices like the mixture-of-experts setup and multi-head latent attention to shrink the KV cache, but it's recognizably the same family of models we had a year or two earlier.

What really shifted was the training recipe after pre-training. A year before, the standard pipeline was pre-training, then supervised instruction fine-tuning, then preference tuning with RLHF or DPO. That made models helpful and pleasant to talk to, but it didn't specifically teach them to work through hard problems step by step. People got some of that with chain-of-thought prompting, but it came from the prompt, not from training.

With R1, and o1 before it from OpenAI, the big idea was that you can use reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. For math or code you can check whether the answer is correct or whether the code compiles and passes tests. You don't need a learned reward model judging style. What I found fascinating about DeepSeek's R1-Zero experiment is that they applied this RL directly to the base model, without a supervised fine-tuning stage first, and reasoning behavior emerged on its own. The model started producing longer chains of thought, checking its work, and backtracking, that "aha moment" they described. Nobody explicitly demonstrated that behavior to it.

The other part is inference-time compute. Instead of only scaling the model and the data, you let the model spend more tokens thinking before it answers, and accuracy goes up on hard tasks. So there are now two knobs: train-time compute and inference-time compute.

And they showed you can distill those reasoning traces into much smaller models and get surprisingly strong results. That made it far more accessible, especially because the weights and a fairly detailed report were open.

So compared to a year earlier, I'd say the "revolution" is less about a new kind of model and more about a new training and inference paradigm. I'd also add a caveat. These models are great at math, coding, and puzzles, where you can verify answers, but you don't need a reasoning model for everything. For a simple factual question or a summary, the extra thinking is often wasted cost and latency, and sometimes they even overthink. It's a specialized tool that's very good at a particular class of problems.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes new training and inference techniques layered onto a recognizable existing transformer model family.

r002.rationale: It says the architecture did not change dramatically and remains recognizably the same family as models from a year or two earlier.

r003.rationale: It explains inference-time compute as letting the model spend more tokens thinking before answering, giving it more time to work through hard problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think the word "revolution" is interesting because it's a bit of a revolution and a bit of a continuation at the same time.

If you think back a year earlier, the dominant paradigm was pretty much: pretrain a big model on as much text as you can, then do supervised fine-tuning on instruction data, then do RLHF with a reward model to align it with human preferences. And the main lever people were pulling was scale. Bigger models, more data, more compute at training time. And honestly, you could already see that lever becoming less effective, or at least more expensive. The gains from going from one generation to the next were getting incremental.

What happened with o1, and then with DeepSeek R1 making it open and documented, was really a shift in where you spend the compute. Instead of only scaling training, you also scale inference. You let the model think longer before it answers. It generates these long chains of thought, it tries approaches, it backtracks, it verifies its own intermediate steps. So the model is effectively doing search at test time, and you can trade more tokens for better answers on hard problems like math and coding.

And the part I found most interesting in the R1 paper was how they got there. With R1-Zero, they took the DeepSeek V3 base model and applied reinforcement learning with essentially just verifiable rewards. Did you get the math problem right, does the code pass the tests, is the output in the right format. No reward model trained on human preferences, no supervised fine-tuning first. And the reasoning behaviors emerged. The long chains of thought, the self-reflection, those "wait, let me reconsider" moments. Nobody wrote those into the training data. That was the real "aha" for a lot of people, including me, because it showed you don't need to hand-curate reasoning traces at scale. You need a good base model and a reliable signal for correctness.

Now, R1-Zero had problems, readability, language mixing, so the full R1 pipeline added a small cold-start SFT stage, then RL, then more SFT with rejection sampling, then RL again. It was a multi-stage recipe, but the engine driving it was RL on verifiable outcomes. And GRPO, their RL algorithm, was a nice simplification over PPO because you drop the separate value model, which made it much more practical.

The other thing that made it a "revolution" rather than just a nice paper is that it was open weights and the report was quite detailed. So within weeks you had people reproducing the core finding on small models, you had the distilled versions showing that you can transfer reasoning into a 7B or 1.5B model through SFT on R1 outputs, and it changed the whole conversation about compute costs because V3 was trained for a fraction of what people assumed frontier models required.

So if I had to summarize it: a year earlier, the question was "how do we make the model bigger and better aligned?" After R1, the question became "how do we teach the model to use more compute productively when it's actually solving the problem?" And the answer turned out to be simpler than most of us expected. Reinforcement learning with a signal that tells you whether the answer is right, applied to a sufficiently strong base model, and you get behaviors that look a lot like reasoning. Whether you want to call it reasoning is a separate philosophical debate, but in terms of capability on hard, checkable tasks, it clearly works.

r001.rationale: The response describes applying reinforcement learning to the existing DeepSeek V3 base model and adding inference-time search.

r002.rationale: The response does not state whether LLM architectures have remained relatively similar over the past year.

r003.rationale: It explains that reasoning involves letting the model think longer and spend more compute at inference time.

astra-6.text:
I think the big shift is that we’re giving models more room to work through a problem before they produce the final answer. A year earlier, the emphasis was largely on making the underlying model better through pretraining and instruction tuning. With reasoning models, there’s another dimension: how much computation you spend at inference time.

And I would separate V3 and R1 a little bit. V3 is the underlying general-purpose model; R1 is about developing reasoning behavior through additional training, particularly reinforcement learning. Instead of prescribing every intermediate step, you can reward a correct outcome on tasks where you can check the answer, like math or coding. That can encourage the model to develop useful intermediate steps, reconsider an approach, and correct mistakes.

What makes this exciting is that it opens up another way to improve performance beyond simply scaling pretraining. But I wouldn’t say reasoning suddenly appeared out of nowhere. We already had chain-of-thought prompting. The change is that working through a problem becomes a behavior the model is trained to use, rather than something we try to elicit with a prompt.

There’s also a tradeoff: longer reasoning takes time and compute, and it doesn’t help equally with every task. So, to me, the revolution is less ‘now models can think’ and more that we have a much more effective way to train and allocate computation for difficult problems.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes V3 as the underlying general-purpose model from R1’s additional training and inference-time computation, describing reasoning as added techniques around a base model.

r002.rationale: It does not state that LLM architectures have remained relatively similar over the past year.

r003.rationale: It directly describes giving models more room and computation at inference time to work through a problem before answering.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the big shift is that we’re giving models more room to work through a problem before producing an answer. A year earlier, a lot of the focus was on making the underlying model stronger through more training data and more compute during training. With reasoning models, we’re also asking: what can we gain by spending more compute at inference time?

I’d distinguish DeepSeek V3 from R1 here. V3 is the underlying general-purpose model, and R1 builds on that foundation with training aimed at reasoning. Reinforcement learning is an important part of that story: for problems where you can check the answer, like certain math and coding tasks, you can reward successful solutions without having a person write out every intermediate step.

What’s interesting is that this can encourage the model to develop behaviors like checking its work, trying another approach, or spending longer on a difficult question. That doesn’t mean the reasoning is always reliable, or that the written explanation gives us a faithful window into everything happening inside the model. But it does change what we can get out of it on tasks that benefit from that extra computation.

So I see it as a substantial advance in training and inference, rather than an entirely new kind of intelligence. And DeepSeek made that advance particularly consequential by releasing model weights that other researchers could study, adapt, and build on.

r001.rationale: It describes R1 as building on V3, the underlying general-purpose model, with reasoning-focused training and reinforcement learning.

r002.rationale: It does not state whether LLM architectures have remained relatively similar over the past year.

r003.rationale: It says reasoning models get more room and inference-time compute to work through problems, including spending longer on difficult questions.
